The reviewers agreed the method is well motivated and novel, the paper is well written, and the experimental section demonstrates the method's effectiveness. The merits of this work outweigh the negative points raised in the reviewer discussion and it is thus clear this work can enrich the conference's program.

Thank you for the in-depth review. Here are our responses to your questions and concerns:

**1. Comparison with Previous Works**

We did not initially compare our work with [1,2] because they are very recent publications. Moreover, a previous version of our paper was also submitted during the ICLR 2025 review period. Therefore, our work and [1,2] were developed contemporaneously. Following the reviewer's suggestion, we have now added a comparison with these two works from both methodological and experimental perspectives.

The main contribution of our work is making the Wasserstein distance an effective measure for encouraging exploration in multi-agent settings. To achieve this, we propose a next-step prediction method based on Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) to learn a trajectory representation space, and we then employ the Wasserstein distance within this latent space. This approach is fundamentally different from the contributions of [1] and [2]. [1] uses a contrastive lower bound to maximize the mutual information between trajectories and learnable identity representations, thereby encouraging multi-agent diversity. This addresses the limitation of previous mutual information methods that tend to overfit to fixed agent identities. In contrast, [2] encourages exploration by maximizing trajectory entropy within a representation space learned by an improved version of SimCLR in a multi-agent setting.

While the representation learning methods of all three works involve contrastive learning, the specific methods employed are distinct. Our work proposes a next-step prediction method based on CPC; [1] uses an improved InfoNCE loss to predict learnable identity representations; and [2] is based on an improved version of SimCLR.

We would also like to clarify that the reviewer's claims (b) and (c) are incorrect. Neither [1] nor [2] involves the Wasserstein Distance (WD), contrary to the reviewer's assertion.

From an experimental perspective, all three works achieve satisfactory performance in certain StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) scenarios. To further compare their performance, we have evaluated all three methods on two additional challenging, sparse-reward SMAC scenarios: so_many_banelings and offence_hard. In so_many_banelings, a reward is given only when the agents win the game. The offence_hard scenario includes advanced environmental obstacles that agents must navigate to strategically engage enemies; rewards are provided only for damaging or eliminating an enemy. The comparison results are shown below:

| Method | so_many_banelings | offence_hard |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| CTR+QMIX [1] | $0.13 \pm 0.06$ | $0.26 \pm 0.11$ |
| TEE+QMIX [2] | $0.21 \pm 0.08$ | $0.37 \pm 0.06$ |
| WCD+QMIX (ours) | $0.63 \pm 0.09$ | $0.75 \pm 0.13$ |

These results show that our method outperforms the other two, demonstrating the effectiveness of maximizing the Wasserstein distance in the learned trajectory representation space.

[1] Li T, Zhu K, Li J, et al. Learning distinguishable trajectory representation with contrastive loss. *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems*, 2024, 37: 64454-64478.

[2] Li T, Zhu K. Toward Efficient Multi-Agent Exploration With Trajectory Entropy Maximization. *The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations*, 2025.

**2. Ethical Concerns**

We note that the reviewer raises significant concerns about the similarity between our work and [3]. Due to the double-blind review policy, we cannot disclose our authorship. The only information we can publicly provide is that, like our submission, [3] is also a paper that was not accepted at ICLR 2025. To fully address this concern, we respectfully request that the Area Chair (AC) confidentially confirm the authorship of our submission and of [3] with the Program Chairs (PC).

[3] Li T., Zhu K. Unsupervised Multi-Agent Diversity With Wasserstein Distance. *Submitted to ICLR 2025.*

Thank you for your careful review and for providing us with detailed and helpful feedback. We respond to your concerns and questions below.

**Weakness 1:** The presented method is mainly the direct combination of existing techniques to address the diversity issue, e.g., CPC for next-step prediction/Trajectory Representation, Wasserstein distance for diversity measurement; the contribution is not significant.

Previous methods based on the Wasserstein distance overlook the similarity of agents’ initial policies resulting from shared policy network parameters, which causes the Wasserstein distance to be an ineffective diversity incentive. To solve this, the main contribution of our work is to enlarge the Wasserstein distance in the latent representation space, making the Wasserstein distance measure effective in multi-agent settings. To learn meaningful representations, we propose employing CPC to contrast different agents' trajectories. Next, we propose a novel kernel method to calculate the Wasserstein distance more efficiently, since directly computing the Wasserstein distance in multi-agent settings is computationally expensive. Moreover, we design a novel intrinsic reward based on the nearest-neighbor Wasserstein distance to efficiently encourage multi-agent diversity. These contributions have not been proposed in previous works.

**Weakness 2:** More importantly, while experimental results are competitive, no theoretical guarantees of the performance are provided.

DiCo provides a theoretical analysis to guarantee that the policies defined by Equation 4 can achieve the desired diversity. Unlike DiCo, we do not directly control diversity. Instead, we enlarge the Wasserstein distance to learn diverse behaviors, solving the issue of inefficient exploration caused by shared policy network parameters. However, such an exploration technique may affect the convergence of the MARL method. Next, we provide a theoretical analysis to guarantee the convergence of the MARL method when our Wasserstein distance-based intrinsic reward is introduced. To achieve this, we theoretically analyze the boundedness of the intrinsic rewards, which is a standard and critical condition for proving convergence. The bounded rewards condition states that the rewards received by the agents at each time step are limited to a finite range. For our intrinsic reward, boundedness ensures that the diversity-seeking objective does not overwhelm the primary goal of maximizing the team reward. If the intrinsic reward were unbounded, it could lead to policies that are arbitrarily diverse but suboptimal in terms of task performance. Specifically, for our proposed WCD method, we prove that the Wasserstein distance-based intrinsic reward is bounded. The boundedness of this intrinsic reward is guaranteed by the properties of the learned representation space and the Wasserstein distance itself.

**1. Boundedness of the Compact Representation Space**

The trajectory representations are guaranteed to be in a compact (i.e., closed and bounded) set due to the architecture of the trajectory encoder. The encoder is composed of a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), both of which use activation functions that constrain their outputs.

Let the trajectory encoder be represented by the function $g_\theta: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{C}$, where $\mathcal{X}$ is the space of trajectory histories and $\mathcal{C}$ is the latent representation space. The encoder is a composition of the non-linear encoder $g_{\theta_e}$ and the autoregressive model $g_{\theta_g}$:

$$c_t^a = g_{\theta_g}(g_{\theta_e}(x_0^a), \dots, g_{\theta_e}(x_{t-1}^a))$$

The boundedness of the output $c_t^a$ can be shown by analyzing the components:

a. **Bounded Activation Functions**: The MLP and GRU components of the encoder use activation functions such as the sigmoid ($\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}$) or the hyperbolic tangent ($\tanh(x)$), which are inherently bounded. For any input $x$, their outputs are confined to a specific range (e.g., $[0, 1]$ for sigmoid, $[-1, 1]$ for tanh).

b. **Bounded Weights and Biases**: During training, the weights and biases of the neural networks are typically regularized (e.g., through weight decay), which keeps them within a finite range.

Given that the inputs to each layer are transformations of the outputs from previous layers with bounded activation functions, the final output of the network, which is the trajectory representation $c_t^a$, will also be bounded. If we assume the maximum possible value for any dimension of the representation vector is $C_{max}$, then the representation space is a subset of a hypercube in $\mathbb{R}^d$:

$$\mathcal{C} \subset [-C_{max}, C_{max}]^d$$

where $d$ is the dimension of the representation space. Since this set is closed and bounded, the representation space is compact.

**2. Boundedness of the Wasserstein Distance**

The Wasserstein distance is used to measure the cost of optimal transport between two probability distributions. When these distributions are defined over a compact set, the Wasserstein distance is also bounded.

The 1-Wasserstein distance has a dual representation known as the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality, which is particularly useful for understanding its properties:

$$W\_1(p, q) = \sup\_{\|f\|\_L \le 1} \left| \mathbb{E}\_{x \sim p}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}\_{y \sim q}[f(y)] \right|$$

where the supremum is taken over all 1-Lipschitz functions $f$.

Let $p$ and $q$ be two probability distributions over the compact representation space $\mathcal{C}$. Since $\mathcal{C}$ is bounded, there exists a constant $M$ such that the distance between any two points $c_1, c_2 \in \mathcal{C}$ is bounded: $d(c_1, c_2) \le M$.

For any 1-Lipschitz function $f$ and any two points $c_1, c_2 \in \mathcal{C}$, we have:
$$|f(c_1) - f(c_2)| \le d(c_1, c_2) \le M$$

Now, consider the expectation of $f$ under the distributions $p$ and $q$:
$$\left| \mathbb{E}\_{x \sim p}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}\_{y \sim q}[f(y)] \right| = \left| \int\_{\mathcal{C}} f(x) dp(x) - \int_{\mathcal{C}} f(y) dq(y) \right|$$

By choosing a reference point $c_0 \in \mathcal{C}$, we can write:
$$\left| \int (f(x) - f(c_0)) dp(x) - \int (f(y) - f(c_0)) dq(y) \right|$$

Since $|f(c) - f(c_0)| \le d(c, c_0) \le M$ for any $c \in \mathcal{C}$, we have:
$$\left| \mathbb{E}\_{x \sim p}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}\_{y \sim q}[f(y)] \right| \le \int M dp(x) + \int M dq(y) = 2M$$

This shows that the Wasserstein distance is bounded, as the distributions are supported on a compact set. The intrinsic reward $r_w$, being the minimum of these bounded distances, is therefore also bounded. This formalizes the boundedness assumption, which is essential for the stability and convergence of the WCD algorithm.

**Weakness 3:** Additionally, more experimental results, especially the comparison with DiCo, can be reported.

The numerical results of the comparisons between WCD+QMIX and DiCo are provided in Tables 1 and 2 in the Appendix, which are clearer than the learning curves. In our work, we compare WCD+QMIX with DiCo on a total of 13 challenging tasks from Pac-Men, SMAC, SMACv2, and GRF.


**Q1:** Although experimental results have been reported to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, there are no theoretical guarantees for the performance improvements.

Please see our response to Weakness 2.

**Q2:** In the paper, the authors claimed that by employing the proposed intrinsic reward function, better performance can be achieved experimentally by keeping the current trajectory away from its nearest neighbor trajectory. However, for tasks that benefit from homogeneity, it may not be true.

In our work, we additionally conduct experiments to investigate whether our method prevents the learning of homogeneous behaviors in the second paragraph of Appendix F.2. This issue is also discussed in lines 253-258 of the main paper. The results demonstrate that our method does not prevent homogeneous behaviors that can lead to higher environmental rewards. Essentially, as discussed in our response to Weakness 2, our method is an exploration technique. In our response to Weakness 2, we theoretically prove that our intrinsic reward is bounded, which ensures the diversity-seeking objective does not overwhelm the primary goal of maximizing the team reward. If the intrinsic reward were unbounded, it could lead to policies that are arbitrarily diverse but suboptimal in terms of task performance. Moreover, as shown in Equation 8, our method only introduces a regularizer to the policy network training, which is weighted by a coefficient $\alpha$.

**Q3:** In the literature, DiCo aims to address the same diversity issue in MARL while theoretically proving the desired diversity can be achieved. Can the proposed method have the same theoretical guarantee? Moreover, more discussions and comparisons about the performances between WCT+QMIX and DiCo can be provided. It is also difficult for me to distinguish the experimental curves representing WCT+QMIX and the experimental curves representing DiCo; they almost have the same color in the experimental figures.

Please see our responses to Weakness 2 and Weakness 3.

**Q4:** How does DiCo perform in terms of exploration, which appears to be missing from the analysis in Figures 8 and 9?

In our work, we do not examine DiCo's performance in terms of exploration. Instead, we compare another similar Wasserstein distance-based method, MAPD. The results demonstrate that MAPD does not yield sufficient exploration of the environment space. Thank you for your valuable suggestion; we have additionally added the visitation heatmap of DiCo to Figures 8 and 9. We note that DiCo also does not lead to sufficient exploration because of its constrained diversity.

During the rebuttal phase, we evaluated the training time in the large-scale 27m_vs_30m scenario (a standard SMAC scenario with the largest number of agents). We ran each method for 5 million steps on the same computational platform. The comparison of training times is shown below:

| Methods | Training time |
|---|---|
| QMIX | 11h 27m 18s |
| WCD+QMIX (ours) | 11h 43m 39s |

The results demonstrate that our method does not significantly increase the training time and scales well with an increasing number of agents. We will further examine our method in large-scale multi-agent tasks with more agents in our future work.


**Q1:** Have you explored or considered task-specific or learned cost functions that might better reflect semantic differences in behavior? How sensitive is WCD to this choice?

We explore the effect of different cost functions on the performance of agents in Appendix J, where we compare the Euclidean distance with cosine similarity, which measures the directional differences between data points. The Wasserstein distance based on cosine similarity achieves slightly better performance in Pac-Men due to the directional characteristics of cosine similarity. The results demonstrate that the final performance of agents is not highly sensitive to the choice of cost function. In our work, we do not specifically discuss different cost functions and use the default Euclidean distance because we want to be consistent with prior works that use the Wasserstein distance to ensure a fair comparison.

**Q2:** See **Weakness 2**.

**Q3:** See **Weakness 3**.

**Q4:** In scenarios where homogeneous behavior is optimal (e.g., focus fire in SMAC), how does WCD avoid hindering convergence to such strategies? Is the nearest-neighbor intrinsic reward turned off or decayed during training, or does it naturally diminish when agents converge?

As discussed in the theoretical analysis in our response to **Weakness 1**, our intrinsic reward is bounded to prevent the diversity-seeking objective from overshadowing the main goal of maximizing the team reward. Thus, our method does not hinder the learning of homogeneous behaviors that are optimal in some scenarios. An unbounded intrinsic reward could result in policies that are highly diverse but ultimately ineffective for the task. Moreover, as shown in Equation 8, we control the influence of our diversity objective relative to the main objective by introducing a weighting coefficient, $\alpha$.


**Q5:** WCD is evaluated only in fully cooperative settings. Can the proposed approach be extended to mixed or competitive MARL environments? If so, how would the diversity metric or reward structure need to be adapted?

The Pac-Men and Google Research Football (GRF) environments used in our work are mixed MARL environments. In Pac-Men, agents may compete for dots if they move to the same room. In GRF, agent-controlled players may compete for the ball to earn more rewards. Our method successfully enables agents to learn optimal policies in these tasks.

rebuttal.value:
We sincerely appreciate your thorough review and valuable feedback on our paper. We answer your questions below:

**Weakness 1: The paper adopts InfoNCE and utilizes next states from other agents to compute the loss. Could the authors provide more insight into the motivation and rationale behind this design choice?**

As we discussed in the first paragraph of Section 3.1, our goal is to distinguish the trajectories of different agents in a latent representation space, enabling the Wasserstein distance to be effective. To achieve this, the InfoNCE loss uses a **contrastive** operation to enable the trajectory representation to stay close to its associated next-step observation-action embedding while being far away from other agents' noisy embeddings. Moreover, predicting the next states helps learn meaningful trajectory representations that are robust to the **noise** in the trajectory sequence, making the learned representations focus on shared, high-level information while discarding local, low-level details and noise.

**Weakness 2: The method requires retraining the trajectory encoder at each step. Does this impact the efficiency of the algorithm? Are there alternative approaches that could allow for encoder reuse to improve efficiency?**

Our method does not retrain the trajectory encoder at each step. During **the** training interval, we train the trajectory encoder to adapt to the sampled trajectory batch before training the **agents' policies**. This helps stabilize training since the trajectories induced by the learning policies can **vary** in different training **phases**. Moreover, the additional computational overhead introduced by our method (including trajectory encoder training and Wasserstein distance computation) is analyzed in **Appendix** K. The **comparison** of training **times** between QMIX and our method demonstrates that our method does not consume **significant** extra training time.

**Weakness 3: The discussion of limitations could be more candid and comprehensive.**

Thank you for your suggestions. We have added the following limitation analysis to the manuscript: We note that our method encourages multi-agent diversity by effectively enlarging the Wasserstein distance in a latent representation space. However, learning trajectory representations using contrastive learning can be **computationally expensive**. Further adaptations of contrastive learning in multi-agent settings need to be considered in future work to make trajectory representation learning more effective and less costly. Moreover, as the number of agents **increases**, the computational cost of the Wasserstein distance objective **grows** significantly, posing a challenge to the scalability of our method.

**Q1: How should the value of $\alpha$ be selected in practice? Does its optimal value depend heavily on specific cases or environments?**

We investigate the effect of the intrinsic reward weight, $\alpha$, on final performance in Appendix I. The results show that our method is not highly sensitive to this value. Sub-optimal weights do not cause a significant performance drop, even in the **most difficult** scenarios. In our experiments, we set the same weight value for the **most difficult** tasks, as the optimal value does not appear to depend heavily on the specific task.

**Q2: What is the motivation for choosing QMIX as the base framework for this work?**

First, QMIX is widely used as the base method in baselines such as EOI, SCDS, and MAVEN. We use the same base method to help **guarantee** a fair **comparison**, which **reduces** the influence of the base method on agent performance. Second, QMIX is fundamental, simple yet efficient, and easy to **integrate**.

**Q3: How is the standard error in the experiments calculated?**

All experimental results are presented as the mean and standard deviation of performance across five random seeds. To calculate the standard deviation, we first compute the mean performance (e.g., win rates in SMAC) over the five random seeds. Then, we find the squared differences from the mean. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance (the average of these squared differences).

summary.value: This paper explores a novel approach to promoting diversity in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). Specifically, the work proposes a method for enhancing trajectory diversity based on the Wasserstein distance. strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths: 
The paper is well-motivated and clearly written,  Wasserstein Contrastive Diversity (WCD) exploration is proposed to promote multi-agent diversity by maximizing the Wasserstein distance between the trajectory distributions of different agents in a latent representation space, and extensive experiments conducted on several multi-agent tasks show the effectiveness of the proposed framework. 

Weakness:
The presented method is mainly the direct combination of existing techniques to address the diversity issue, e.g., CPC for next-step prediction/Trajectory Representation, Wasserstein distance for diversity measurement, the contribution is not significant. More importantly, while experimental results are competitive, no theoretical guarantees of the performance are provided. Additionally, more experimental results, especially the comparison with DiCo, can be reported.

questions.value:
1. Although experimental results have been reported to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, there are no theoretical guarantees for the performance improvements. 
2. In the paper, the authors claimed that by employing the proposed intrinsic reward function, better performance can be achieved experimentally by keeping the current trajectory away from its nearest neighbor trajectory. However, for tasks that benefit from homogeneity, it may not be true. 
3. In the literature, DiCo aims to address the same diversity issue in MARL while theoretically proving the desired diversity can be achieved. Can the proposed method have the same theoretical guarantee? Moreover, more discussions and comparisons about the performances between WCT+QMIX and DiCo can be provided. It is also difficult for me to distinguish the experimental curves representing WCT+QMIX and the experimental curves representing DiCo, they almost have the same color in the experimental figures. 
4. How does DiCo perform in terms of exploration, which appears to be missing from the analysis in Figures 8 and 9?

summary.value: This paper proposes Wasserstein Contrastive Diversity (WCD), a method to promote diverse behaviors in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), especially under shared policy networks. WCD learns contrastive trajectory representations via Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) and maximizes the Wasserstein distance between agent trajectories in this latent space. This encourages meaningful behavioral diversity. The method integrates efficiently with algorithms like QMIX and MAPPO using a nearest-neighbor intrinsic reward. Experiments on challenging MARL benchmarks show that WCD significantly improves exploration and overall performance.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
## Strength

- Clear motivation. The paper addresses a well-known limitation in cooperative MARL,l ack of agent diversity under shared policy network and motivates the use of metric-aware approaches like Wasserstein distance to overcome it.

- The method is shown to integrate seamlessly with both value-based (QMIX) and policy-based (MAPPO) MARL algorithms, increasing its practical applicability.

## Weakness

- While the method is empirically sound, the paper lacks deeper theoretical analysis (e.g., convergence guarantees, diversity-exploration trade-offs), which could strengthen its foundation.

- The representation learning relies heavily on CPC and InfoNCE loss. If CPC fails to capture meaningful distinctions in more complex domains, WCD’s effectiveness could degrade

- Although kernel methods reduce cost, computing pairwise Wasserstein distances (even with nearest-neighbor selection) could still be expensive in very large-scale multi-agent systems.

questions.value:
- The authors adopt the Euclidean distance in the latent trajectory representation space as the cost function for the Wasserstein computation. Have you explored or considered task-specific or learned cost functions that might better reflect semantic differences in behavior? How sensitive is WCD to this choice?

- Since the effectiveness of WCD heavily depends on CPC for producing distinguishable trajectory embeddings, how robust is the method when CPC representations are noisy or collapse in more complex observation spaces (e.g., continuous control with high-dimensional inputs)? 

- While your kernel-based approach improves efficiency over dual-network parametrization, computing Wasserstein distances across many agent pairs may still be costly. Can you provide runtime and memory analysis for scalability when the number of agents grows significantly (e.g., >50 agents)?

- In scenarios where homogeneous behavior is optimal (e.g., focus fire in SMAC), how does WCD avoid hindering convergence to such strategies? Is the nearest-neighbor intrinsic reward turned off or decayed during training, or does it naturally diminish when agents converge?

- WCD is evaluated only in fully cooperative settings. Can the proposed approach be extended to mixed or competitive MARL environments? If so, how would the diversity metric or reward structure need to be adapted?

This paper addresses the challenge of insufficient exploration in cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), where agents with shared policy parameters tend to learn similar behaviors, resulting in suboptimal cooperation.

title.value: Encouraging metric-aware diversity in contrastive representation space

abstract.value: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents that share policy network parameters often learn similar behaviors, which hinders effective exploration and can lead to suboptimal cooperative policies. Recent advances have attempted to promote multi-agent diversity by leveraging the Wasserstein distance to increase policy differences. However, these methods cannot effectively encourage diverse policies due to ineffective Wasserstein distance caused by the policy similarity. To address this limitation, we propose Wasserstein Contrastive Diversity (WCD) exploration, a novel approach that promotes multi-agent diversity by maximizing the Wasserstein distance between the trajectory distributions of different agents in a latent representation space. To make the Wasserstein distance meaningful, we propose a novel next-step prediction method based on Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) to learn distinguishable trajectory representations. Additionally, we introduce an optimized kernel-based method to compute the Wasserstein distance more efficiently. Since the Wasserstein distance is inherently defined for two distributions, we extend it to support multiple agents, enabling diverse policy learning. Empirical evaluations across a variety of challenging multi-agent tasks demonstrate that WCD outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, delivering superior performance and enhanced exploration.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/ ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
